lines: A big table is about to join the result of grouping another big table down to a tiny number of rows.
Before a single task runs, what does the planner even commit to?
Here's the measured plan, captured before any shuffle has run.
Both sides get sorted, then merged. That's the planner's own default for two large tables joined on equality.
But notice what it doesn't know yet: the real size of that grouped result. All it has is the size of the table going into the grouping, which is large.
That grouping still has to shuffle its own rows to finish counting them.
The moment it does, Spark has a real number for how many rows came out.
Does the join sitting above it, which hasn't run yet, get a second look with that number in hand?
steps.answer: It does. A shuffle boundary is the one moment every partition's real size exists before the next step runs, and Spark takes that moment to reconsider.

lines: Here's the plan after that reconsideration.
The sort-merge strategy is gone completely. The now-known-tiny side gets broadcast instead, and the other side reads its own shuffle output locally rather than sorting and merging anything.
Same query, same data, a different strategy chosen only once the truth about one side's size existed.
Nothing about the join operator itself changed between those two plans.
What changed is that a number existed which simply didn't exist before: the grouped side's real, tiny size.
That's the number the broadcast threshold is checked against, and it only existed once the grouping had actually run.
Switch to a different query entirely. This one is configured with two hundred shuffle partitions from the start, the way a lot of real queries are.
Nobody sized that number to the data; it's just a session-wide default somebody set once.
If the real work barely needs a handful of partitions, does Spark still run two hundred separate tasks anyway?
steps.answer: No. The same reconsideration that can swap a join's strategy can also merge small partitions together once their real sizes are known.

lines: Look at the two plans side by side.
The version captured before any shuffle has nothing resembling a merge step for those partitions. It simply commits to the configured count.
Only the version captured after the shuffle shows the small partitions actually combined before whatever reads them next.
That configured count of two hundred was never actually sized to this data; nobody tuned it for this particular query.
The number that ended up running came from somewhere else entirely: the shuffle's own real output, measured after the fact.
Nobody has to guess a shuffle-partition count correctly up front anymore for this to work.
Both of today's examples share the same shape. Something runs, a shuffle boundary is crossed, and only then does Spark get to rewrite what comes next.

That also marks the edge of what this can touch: whatever already happened before that first boundary, the scan, the filter, the initial projection, is already done. No amount of reconsidering later changes it.
